options.a: A fresh-water rinse and wipe of the bowl
options.b: Disinfection at the end of the day only
options.c: Cleaning and disinfection of jets/filters
options.d: Cleaning of the bowl surface, not the jets

distractorExplanations.a: Rinsing removes visible debris but kills nothing; the basin and jets need cleaning plus EPA disinfectant contact time.
distractorExplanations.b: End-of-day deep cleaning is an extra step; basins must still be cleaned and disinfected after every client.
distractorExplanations.d: Biofilm grows inside whirlpool pipes and filters, so skipping the jets leaves the main infection source untouched.

options.a: Sprayed with disinfectant, then wiped dry
options.b: Disinfected first, then scrubbed clean
options.c: Wiped with an alcohol pad between clients
options.d: Cleaned of debris, then fully disinfected

distractorExplanations.a: Skips the cleaning step and the label contact time; debris blocks disinfectant and wiping ends contact early.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the order: debris must be removed first or the disinfectant cannot reach the metal surface.
distractorExplanations.c: A quick wipe is not full immersion for the label contact time and skips cleaning off debris first.

options.a: The tech from fungi and chemicals, and the client from your skin flora
options.b: The client from tool cuts, but not the tech from chemicals or fungus
options.c: The tech from chemicals only; fungi cannot pass through intact skin
options.d: Neither party once tools are disinfected, so gloves are optional

distractorExplanations.b: Gloves do not stop sharp-tool cuts; their main role is to shield the tech from pathogens and chemicals and the client from the tech.
distractorExplanations.c: Fungi and other pathogens spread through tiny skin breaks, so gloves protect against microbes as well as chemicals.
distractorExplanations.d: Tool disinfection does not protect hands from the client's skin, fluids, or chemicals; gloves are standard on feet.

options.a: Filed thin and treated with an antifungal polish you sell
options.b: Referred to a physician; do not push a 'fungus bit'
options.c: Serviced normally if the client signs a waiver first
options.d: Covered with gel so the fungus is sealed off from air

distractorExplanations.a: Treating a suspected infection is medical care outside nail-tech scope; filing also spreads the fungus.
distractorExplanations.c: A waiver does not make servicing an infected nail safe or legal; it still spreads infection to tools and others.
distractorExplanations.d: Covering a fungal nail traps moisture and hides the infection, worsening it rather than sealing it off.

options.a: Disinfected and reused for the next client
options.b: Stored in a labeled bag for that client
options.c: Discarded after the client
options.d: Rinsed in the pedicure basin, then dried

distractorExplanations.a: Foam separators are porous and cannot be disinfected, so boards classify them as single-use.
distractorExplanations.b: Keeping porous single-use items for a client's next visit is not allowed; they go to the client or the trash.
distractorExplanations.d: Rinsing in the basin neither cleans nor disinfects porous foam and can spread contamination to the bowl.

options.a: Cure gels matched to their wavelength
options.b: Require periodic bulb replacement
options.c: Emit ultraviolet or near-UV light
options.d: Replace disinfection of metal tools

distractorExplanations.a: Curing matched gels is exactly what a UV/LED lamp does, so it does not fit 'do not'.
distractorExplanations.b: UV bulbs and LED diodes lose output over time and do need replacement, so this is something lamps do.
distractorExplanations.c: Both UV and LED nail lamps emit UVA or near-UV light to trigger photoinitiators, so this is true of them.

options.a: Before and after each client and after glove removal
options.b: Before each service, with gloves replacing it afterward
options.c: At the start of each shift and after eating or smoking
options.d: Only when hands look visibly soiled after a service

distractorExplanations.b: Gloves can tear and hands get contaminated when removing them, so handwashing is still required after glove removal.
distractorExplanations.c: Shift-start and break handwashing are good habits but do not replace washing before and after every client.
distractorExplanations.d: Pathogens are invisible; handwashing is required before and after each client whether or not hands look dirty.

options.a: Clean emery boards kept for the next client
options.b: Used blades, bits, and bloody disposables
options.c: Empty product bottles and packaging
options.d: Laundered towels and unused cotton rounds

distractorExplanations.a: Unused or client-kept files are not sharps or blood waste; the covered disposal plan is for contaminated items.
distractorExplanations.c: Empty containers are routine trash or recycling, not sharps or blood-contaminated waste.
distractorExplanations.d: Clean linens and unused cotton carry no contamination and do not need a sharps or bloodborne disposal plan.

options.a: Wiped with acetone and reused on the next client
options.b: Disinfected first, then brushed clean of debris
options.c: Brushed, then disinfected or sterilized
options.d: Rinsed in water and left to air-dry

distractorExplanations.a: Acetone removes product but is not an EPA-registered disinfectant, so the bit is still contaminated.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the order: product dust must be brushed off before disinfection or the disinfectant cannot reach the metal.
distractorExplanations.d: Water rinsing removes some dust but does not disinfect; bits contacting the plate need full disinfection.

options.a: Do not work over it; refer out
options.b: Cover it with a bandage and continue
options.c: File it down gently with a fine buffer
options.d: Service it last, then disinfect tools

distractorExplanations.b: Warts are contagious viral growths; covering one does not make it safe to work on that area.
distractorExplanations.c: Filing a wart spreads the virus and treats a medical condition, which is outside nail-tech scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Scheduling a client last does not make working over an infectious wart acceptable; refer instead.

options.a: Disinfectant residue is not left on feet
options.b: Skin cells and fungus are not shared
options.c: The basin stays dry between clients
options.d: Towels can go back on the shelf unwashed if dry

distractorExplanations.a: Residue is a rinsing issue; fresh towels are about not passing skin cells and fungus between clients.
distractorExplanations.c: Basin drying is part of bowl cleaning; towels are single-client to stop cross-contamination.
distractorExplanations.d: A used towel carries skin cells and fungal spores even when dry; it must be laundered before reuse.

options.a: The official NIC written exam released for practice
options.b: A state board licensing exam scored for credit
options.c: Independent UniPrep practice — not a state board written
options.d: A retired PSI state board form shared by the board

distractorExplanations.a: NIC does not release live written forms; this is an independent practice set, not an official exam.
distractorExplanations.b: This practice mock earns no licensing credit; only the board's proctored written exam counts.
distractorExplanations.d: This is not a PSI or board-released form; it is independent UniPrep practice written to the content areas.

options.a: The living tissue that produces new nail cells
options.b: The soft skin that seals the plate at its base
options.c: The skin layer beneath that supplies blood
options.d: The visible hard keratin you file and enhance

distractorExplanations.a: That describes the matrix; the nail plate itself is hardened keratin with no living cells.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes the eponychium/cuticle area, not the hard plate you file and enhance.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes the nail bed, which lies under the plate and is rich in blood vessels.

options.a: The growth area under the proximal fold
options.b: The skin under the free edge that seals it
options.c: The skin directly beneath the nail plate
options.d: The dead tissue that sticks to the plate

distractorExplanations.b: That describes the hyponychium, the seal under the free edge, not the growth area.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes the nail bed; the matrix sits under the proximal fold and produces the plate.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes the cuticle, which is dead tissue; the matrix is living tissue that makes new nail.

options.a: The skin fold at the base
options.b: The seal under the free edge
options.c: The dead tissue lifted off the plate
options.d: The fold of skin along the nail sides

distractorExplanations.a: The skin at the base of the nail is the eponychium/proximal fold, not the hyponychium under the free edge.
distractorExplanations.c: Dead tissue lifted off the plate is the cuticle; the hyponychium is living skin under the free edge.
distractorExplanations.d: Skin along the sides is the lateral nail fold (sidewall), not the hyponychium seal under the tip.

options.a: Thickening of the nail plate
options.b: Inflammation of the nail folds
options.c: Separation of plate from bed
options.d: Shedding of the whole nail

distractorExplanations.a: Abnormal thickening is onychauxis; onycholysis is the plate lifting away from the bed.
distractorExplanations.b: Inflamed nail folds describe paronychia, an infection of the surrounding skin, not plate separation.
distractorExplanations.d: Complete shedding of the nail is onychomadesis/onychoptosis, not onycholysis, which starts at the free edge.

options.a: Dead tissue on the nail plate
options.b: Seal under free edge
options.c: The nail's growth center
options.d: Living skin at the base

distractorExplanations.a: Dead tissue stuck to the plate is the cuticle; the eponychium is living skin and must not be cut.
distractorExplanations.b: The seal under the free edge is the hyponychium, at the opposite end of the nail from the eponychium.
distractorExplanations.c: The growth center is the matrix under the proximal fold, not the visible living skin at the base.

options.a: A bruise under the plate — refer if severe or painful
options.b: A fungal infection to treat with an antifungal soak
options.c: A dark gel stain to buff out of the plate surface
options.d: A pseudomonas 'greenie' to cover with fresh product

distractorExplanations.b: A dark nail right after trauma points to a bruise (hematoma); treating fungus is also outside nail-tech scope.
distractorExplanations.c: A blue-black discoloration after injury lies under the plate, so buffing the surface cannot remove it.
distractorExplanations.d: Pseudomonas shows green, not blue-black after trauma, and covering any discoloration hides a problem.

options.a: Vertical ridges that increase with age
options.b: Horizontal ridges after illness or trauma
options.c: White spots from minor injury to the matrix
options.d: Spoon-shaped nails linked to iron deficiency

distractorExplanations.a: Vertical (longitudinal) ridges are common with aging; Beau's lines run horizontally across the plate.
distractorExplanations.c: White spots from minor trauma are leukonychia, not the horizontal grooves of Beau's lines.
distractorExplanations.d: Spoon-shaped nails are koilonychia; Beau's lines are horizontal ridges after illness or trauma.

options.a: The growth area under the proximal nail fold
options.b: The skin seal beneath the free edge
options.c: The skin under the plate rich in blood vessels
options.d: The living skin fold at the base of the nail

distractorExplanations.a: The growth area under the proximal fold is the matrix, not the nail bed under the plate.
distractorExplanations.b: The seal beneath the free edge is the hyponychium; the nail bed lies under the attached plate.
distractorExplanations.d: The living skin at the base is the eponychium, not the vascular bed the plate rests on.

options.a: White, chalky patches on the plate surface
options.b: Skin stuck to the plate
options.c: Thick, curved nails with yellow edges
options.d: Red, swollen skin around the nail

distractorExplanations.a: Chalky white patches on the plate suggest superficial fungus or leukonychia, not paronychia of the skin folds.
distractorExplanations.b: Skin adhering to and growing onto the plate is a pterygium, not the inflamed folds of paronychia.
distractorExplanations.c: Thick, curved nails describe onychogryphosis; paronychia is inflammation of the surrounding skin.

options.a: Abnormal skin adhesion on the plate
options.b: Separation of the plate from the bed
options.c: Inflammation of the skin around the nail
options.d: Normal dead cuticle you push back

distractorExplanations.b: Plate separating from the bed is onycholysis; a pterygium is skin abnormally adhering to the plate.
distractorExplanations.c: Inflamed skin around the nail is paronychia, an infection, not the abnormal skin growth of a pterygium.
distractorExplanations.d: Normal cuticle is dead tissue that lifts away; a pterygium is living skin and must not be pushed or torn.

options.a: The skin seal under the nail tip
options.b: The part that extends past the finger
options.c: The pale half-moon at the base
options.d: The nail's side borders in the grooves

distractorExplanations.a: The skin seal under the tip is the hyponychium, which must be protected, not filed.
distractorExplanations.c: The pale half-moon at the base is the lunula, the visible part of the matrix, not the free edge.
distractorExplanations.d: The side borders sit in the lateral grooves (sidewalls); the free edge is the tip past the fingertip.

options.a: A sign of onychomycosis that needs referral
options.b: Removed by a bleach soak you recommend
options.c: Usually cosmetic; fungus is a different picture
options.d: A sign of matrix damage needing medical care

distractorExplanations.a: Polish staining is surface discoloration; fungus shows thickening, crumbling, or debris, not just yellow tint.
distractorExplanations.b: Recommending bleach soaks is unsafe and outside scope; staining fades as the plate grows out or with base coat use.
distractorExplanations.d: Matrix damage changes the shape or growth of new nail; polish stain sits on the plate surface.

options.a: Trimmed into the corner to relieve it
options.b: Lifted with cotton and covered with gel
options.c: Soaked, then filed down at the edge
options.d: Left to a medical professional

distractorExplanations.a: Cutting into the corner of an inflamed ingrown is a medical procedure and risks deeper infection.
distractorExplanations.b: Packing and covering an inflamed nail treats a medical condition and can trap infection; refer instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Soaking and filing an inflamed ingrown still works on infected tissue, which is outside nail-tech scope.

options.a: The protein of hair and nails
options.b: The lipid that keeps nails flexible
options.c: Calcium, the nail hardener
options.d: The living cells of the nail matrix

distractorExplanations.b: Lipids help flexibility, but keratin is a fibrous protein, the main structural material of hair and nails.
distractorExplanations.c: Nails are hard because of keratin protein, not calcium; calcium content in nails is minimal.
distractorExplanations.d: Matrix cells produce keratin, but keratin itself is the protein those cells fill with as they harden.

options.a: Polish, shape, cuticle work, sanitize, nourish
options.b: Shape, sanitize, polish, then cuticle work
options.c: Sanitize, shape, cuticle work, nourish, polish
options.d: Cuticle work, sanitize, shape, polish, nourish

distractorExplanations.a: Hand sanitizing comes first, and polish goes last; polishing before shaping and cuticle work wrecks the finish.
distractorExplanations.b: Sanitizing must come before shaping, and cuticle work is done before polish, not after it.
distractorExplanations.d: Starting with cuticle work before sanitizing skips infection control, and nourishing oil goes before polish.

options.a: Lets you safely trim the living eponychium at the base
options.b: Disinfects the cuticle area before nipping
options.c: Hardens the cuticle so it clips cleanly
options.d: Softens only dead tissue you are allowed to remove

distractorExplanations.a: Softening does not make live tissue safe to cut; trimming the eponychium is cutting living skin.
distractorExplanations.b: A soak softens tissue but is not a disinfectant step; implements still need proper disinfection.
distractorExplanations.c: Soaking softens rather than hardens tissue, which is why only dead cuticle should then be removed.

options.a: Applied thin and cured per the lamp and product
options.b: Applied in one thick coat and cured for a longer time
options.c: Applied thin and air-dried like lacquer
options.d: Cured in any UV or LED lamp for 2 minutes

distractorExplanations.b: Thick coats wrinkle and undercure at the bottom even with longer curing; gel goes on in thin layers.
distractorExplanations.c: Gel polish does not air-dry; it needs a lamp to trigger its photoinitiators.
distractorExplanations.d: Cure time and lamp type depend on the product's photoinitiators; a mismatched lamp undercures.

options.a: Pry the gel off once it lifts
options.b: Use the product's method
options.c: Buff off all gel with a coarse grit
options.d: Soak in warm water to loosen it

distractorExplanations.a: Prying gel off strips layers of the nail plate; follow the product's soak-off method.
distractorExplanations.c: Coarse grits over the full gel risk thinning the natural plate; break the seal lightly and soak per the maker.
distractorExplanations.d: Water does not dissolve soak-off gel; most systems use acetone per the manufacturer's directions.

options.a: Repairing a cracked enhancement at the stress area
options.b: Replacing the whole enhancement each visit
options.c: Regrowth at the cuticle area of an enhancement
options.d: Adding length to the free edge of the nail

distractorExplanations.a: Fixing a crack is a repair; a fill rebalances regrowth near the cuticle area.
distractorExplanations.b: Full removal and reapplication is a new set; a fill only addresses regrowth and rebalances.
distractorExplanations.d: Adding length is an extension or tip service, not a fill of the regrowth area at the cuticle.

options.a: Remove oil and moisture from the plate
options.b: Seal the finished enhancement against lifting
options.c: Thin the monomer for a smoother bead
options.d: Help enhancement adhesion on a prepared plate

distractorExplanations.a: Removing oil and moisture is the dehydrator's job; primer helps the product bond after that prep.
distractorExplanations.b: Sealing the finished surface is done with top coat or sealer gel, not primer on the bare plate.
distractorExplanations.c: Primer is applied to the plate, not mixed into monomer; bead consistency comes from liquid-to-powder ratio.

options.a: Stay light, with the correct bit and RPM
options.b: Run at top RPM to finish before heat builds
options.c: Use a coarse carbide bit to thin the plate
options.d: Press firmly so the bit stays in one spot

distractorExplanations.b: High RPM on the natural plate generates friction heat faster; speed should match the bit and task.
distractorExplanations.c: Coarse carbide bits are for product removal; on the natural plate they thin and damage the nail.
distractorExplanations.d: Pressure and dwelling in one spot cause heat spikes and rings of damage; keep the bit moving lightly.

options.a: The pale half-moon of the matrix at the base
options.b: A design on the free edge, not a medical term
options.c: A white band caused by lifting at the free edge
options.d: A ridge across the plate left by e-file damage

distractorExplanations.a: The pale half-moon at the base is the lunula; the smile line is the curved design line at the free edge.
distractorExplanations.c: Product lifting shows as a white or cloudy gap, not as the deliberate curve painted in a French design.
distractorExplanations.d: E-file damage leaves rings or grooves in the plate; the smile line is a polish design feature.

options.a: Light effleurage on the calf and foot
options.b: Any contact above the ankle bone
options.c: Broken skin, varicose-vein issues, and deep work
options.d: Pressure checks with the client during massage

distractorExplanations.a: Light effleurage is standard comfort massage in a pedicure; it is not something to avoid on healthy skin.
distractorExplanations.b: Pedicure massage commonly includes the lower leg; the concern is broken skin, flagged veins, and deep work.
distractorExplanations.d: Asking about pressure is good practice for comfort and safety, not something to avoid.

options.a: Rounded into the corners to reduce ingrowns
options.b: Cut short to the hyponychium for neatness
options.c: Cut with a V-notch in the center
options.d: Straight across to reduce ingrowns

distractorExplanations.a: Rounding into the corners encourages ingrown nails; toenails are cut straight across.
distractorExplanations.b: Cutting down to the hyponychium removes the protective free edge and raises injury and ingrown risk.
distractorExplanations.c: The V-notch is a folk myth; it does not stop ingrowns, while straight-across trimming does.

options.a: Cutting into the groove risks injury and infection
options.b: Short nails prevent all ingrowns, so it is fine
options.c: Filing to the bed is safe if you skip nippers
options.d: It is fine if you soak the toes first

distractorExplanations.b: Cutting too short into the groove actually increases ingrown risk as the corner grows into the skin.
distractorExplanations.c: Filing down to the bed exposes skin and invites injury and infection just as cutting does.
distractorExplanations.d: Soaking softens the nail but does not make cutting into the groove safe; the injury risk remains.

options.a: Extra adhesive to seal the lifted edge
options.b: Water and microbes — remove and rebalance
options.c: A top coat layer to keep product on
options.d: Oils that strengthen the natural plate

distractorExplanations.a: Gluing down lifted product traps water and microbes underneath; the lifted area must be removed and rebalanced.
distractorExplanations.c: Top coat over a lift seals in moisture and bacteria; it does not reattach lifted product.
distractorExplanations.d: Gaps under lifted product collect water and microbes, not beneficial oils; that is how 'greenies' start.

options.a: Warmed slightly so the bead sets faster
options.b: Poured back into the original bottle after the service
options.c: Used in a well-ventilated area with the lid managed
options.d: Disposed of by pouring it down the drain

distractorExplanations.a: Heating monomer increases flammable vapors; it is used at room temperature with good ventilation.
distractorExplanations.b: Used monomer is contaminated with powder and debris; returning it spoils the whole bottle.
distractorExplanations.d: Monomer must not go down the drain; leftovers are absorbed and sealed per the SDS and local rules.

options.a: Shared between clients without cleaning
options.b: Disinfected by dipping in monomer
options.c: Stored wet in acetone between clients
options.d: Cleaned of product; it is not a sanitizer

distractorExplanations.a: Brushes touch product on each client's nails and must be cleaned of product between clients.
distractorExplanations.b: Monomer cleans acrylic out of a brush but is not an EPA-registered disinfectant.
distractorExplanations.c: Acetone damages brush bristles and is not a disinfectant; brushes are cleaned of product and stored dry.

options.a: Follow product labels and not give medical advice
options.b: Tell her that all nail chemicals are safe
options.c: Refuse every service until after delivery
options.d: Recommend a pregnancy-safe supplement list to the client

distractorExplanations.b: Making safety guarantees is medical advice; follow labels and refer pregnancy questions to her physician.
distractorExplanations.c: Pregnancy is not a blanket contraindication; services proceed per product labels and client comfort.
distractorExplanations.d: Recommending supplements during pregnancy is medical advice and outside nail-tech scope.

options.a: The standard monomer in most salon acrylic kits
options.b: Banned or heavily restricted for nails in many states
options.c: Allowed if the salon has local exhaust ventilation
options.d: A gentler monomer that soaks off more easily

distractorExplanations.a: EMA (ethyl methacrylate) is the standard salon monomer; MMA is the restricted one.
distractorExplanations.c: Ventilation does not lift the restriction; MMA bonds too hard and is banned for nail use in many states.
distractorExplanations.d: MMA is harder and resists acetone soak-off, which is part of why it damages the natural plate.

options.a: A UV or LED lamp to cure the bead
options.b: A dehydrator in place of primer
options.c: Correct liquid-to-powder ratio
options.d: An extra-wet bead for strength

distractorExplanations.a: Lamp curing is for gels; EMA acrylic cures by chemical polymerization once liquid and powder mix.
distractorExplanations.b: Dehydrator and primer do different jobs; EMA work depends on the correct liquid-to-powder ratio.
distractorExplanations.d: A wet bead runs into the cuticle and weakens the cured product; the ratio must be balanced.

options.a: Disinfect the plate before application
options.b: Replace the dehydrator step
options.c: Cure faster under an LED lamp
options.d: Burn skin if it runs off the plate

distractorExplanations.a: Acid primer improves adhesion; it is not an EPA disinfectant for the plate or tools.
distractorExplanations.b: Dehydrator removes oil and moisture first; primer is a separate adhesion step and does not replace it.
distractorExplanations.c: Acrylic primer is not light-cured; its hazard is chemical burns if it runs onto skin.

options.a: Timed and buffered so skin is not macerated raw
options.b: Left on overnight under foil for easy removal
options.c: Warmed over a heat source to speed removal
options.d: Done after filing the gel down to the bed

distractorExplanations.b: Prolonged acetone contact dehydrates and macerates the skin; soak-off should be timed per the product.
distractorExplanations.c: Acetone is highly flammable; heating it near a flame or hot plate is a fire hazard.
distractorExplanations.d: Filing down to the natural plate thins it; break the top seal lightly and let acetone do the work.

options.a: The lamp's wattage alone, not wavelength
options.b: The gel's photoinitiators matching the lamp
options.c: The thickness of the base coat used
options.d: The brand of top coat over the gel

distractorExplanations.a: Wattage is not the deciding factor; the lamp's wavelength must match the gel's photoinitiators.
distractorExplanations.c: Layer thickness affects cure depth, but whether LED or UV works depends on photoinitiator match.
distractorExplanations.d: Top coat brand does not decide lamp compatibility; each gel's photoinitiators must match the lamp.

options.a: Extra shine and flexibility
options.b: Heat spikes during curing
options.c: Allergy and peeling
options.d: Yellowing from UV exposure

distractorExplanations.a: Undercured gel stays soft and tacky; it does not add shine or useful flexibility.
distractorExplanations.b: Heat spikes come from thick layers or strong lamps during cure, not from leaving gel undercured.
distractorExplanations.d: Yellowing relates to UV aging or product quality; the key undercure risk is allergy and peeling.

options.a: A dehydrator that preps the plate
options.b: A softener that disinfects the cuticle
options.c: A primer that improves adhesion
options.d: A conditioner for skin and plate

distractorExplanations.a: Dehydrators remove oil before enhancements; cuticle oil adds oil and would hurt adhesion if used first.
distractorExplanations.b: Cuticle oil softens and conditions but has no disinfecting action on skin or tools.
distractorExplanations.c: Primer promotes bonding of product; oil on the plate does the opposite and causes lifting.

options.a: Change cure and cause lifting or allergy
options.b: Strengthen the gel's chemical bond to the plate
options.c: Speed up curing under an LED lamp
options.d: Replace the need for a top coat

distractorExplanations.b: Foreign particles interrupt the gel's polymer network; they weaken it rather than strengthen it.
distractorExplanations.c: Glitter blocks light, so cure slows and may be incomplete, which leads to lifting and allergy.
distractorExplanations.d: Added glitter does not seal the surface; the system still needs its tested top coat.

options.a: The product is old and losing strength
options.b: Ventilate and cap the liquid
options.c: Mask the smell with a scented candle
options.d: Use more liquid for a wetter bead

distractorExplanations.a: Odor signals vapor in the air, not weak product; the fix is ventilation and capping the liquid.
distractorExplanations.c: An open flame near flammable monomer vapor is a fire hazard, and masking odor does not remove vapor.
distractorExplanations.d: More liquid releases more vapor and makes a runny bead; it worsens the problem.

options.a: Bonding the product to the nail plate
options.b: Disinfecting the plate before service
options.c: Removing oil from the plate before enhancement
options.d: Sealing and protecting the finished enhancement surface

distractorExplanations.a: Bonding is the primer's role; dehydrator removes oil and moisture before primer goes on.
distractorExplanations.b: Dehydrator is a prep chemical, not a disinfectant; it removes surface oils.
distractorExplanations.d: Sealing the finished surface is a top coat's job; dehydrator is used before product is applied.

options.a: Labeled, upright, away from heat and kids
options.b: In unlabeled spray bottles at each station
options.c: In a warm cabinet so liquids stay fluid
options.d: Decanted into smaller food containers

distractorExplanations.b: Hazard communication rules require every container to be labeled with its contents.
distractorExplanations.c: Heat increases vapor and fire risk for monomers and acetone; store away from heat.
distractorExplanations.d: Food containers invite accidental ingestion and lack hazard labels; keep chemicals in labeled containers.

options.a: Only products labeled as flammable
options.b: Monomers, primers, acetone, and disinfectants
options.c: Implements such as nippers, pushers, and e-file bits
options.d: Client medical history and allergies

distractorExplanations.a: SDS are required for every hazardous chemical in the salon, not just flammable ones.
distractorExplanations.c: SDS cover chemical products, not metal implements; tools fall under disinfection rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Client history belongs on intake forms; SDS describe the hazards of the salon's chemicals.

options.a: The polish is free of all chemicals
options.b: The polish is safe for allergy-prone clients
options.c: Certain chemicals were left out
options.d: The polish is approved by the FDA

distractorExplanations.a: Every polish is made of chemicals; '3-free' or '5-free' means specific named ingredients were omitted.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaving out a few ingredients does not make a polish hypoallergenic; other allergens may remain.
distractorExplanations.d: FDA does not approve cosmetics before sale; 'X-free' is a marketing label, not an approval.

options.a: A hard-surface disinfectant where the label and board allow
options.b: A laundry additive for salon towels
options.c: A diluted floor cleaner per the label
options.d: A routine nail soak or 'fungus treatment'

distractorExplanations.a: Diluted bleach is an accepted surface disinfectant when the label and board rules allow, so it is not the 'never' use.
distractorExplanations.b: Bleach is a normal laundry additive for salon linens, so this use is acceptable.
distractorExplanations.c: Label-directed floor cleaning is an acceptable bleach use; soaking client nails in it is the unsafe one.
